text: You've already chosen your KPIs back in the last lesson. Now the real question: where do they actually go on the page, and why does that placement matter as much as the numbers themselves?

Most audiences read top to bottom, left to right, without even thinking about it — so the single most important, highest-level fact goes in the top-left corner, with detail increasing naturally as the eye moves right and down from there. A card visual is one of the simplest ways to make one number completely impossible to miss. Size alone does the communicating here — a number rendered large reads as more important before anyone's even consciously processed what it means.

Here's that exact principle applied in a real, finished dashboard. Total Volume sits top-left — the single highest-level number on the entire page. Moving right and down from there: a trend line, a segment breakdown, a manufacturer-by-region treemap, each one progressively more specific than the last. Nothing here is accidental — it's the reading-order principle, applied directly and deliberately.

And everything has to fit cleanly on one screen, with absolutely no scrollbars — if it doesn't fit, that's usually a sign some of that content belongs on a full report page instead. Keep scales, axis ordering, and color usage consistent across every tile, so nobody has to relearn what a color means from one tile to the next. Next: storytelling with data — choosing visuals that genuinely support the point you're trying to make, rather than just showing off variety.
